claims.text: The target material is bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing intrinsic defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A hybrid ab initio and machine-learning approach will significantly reduce electrical-conductivity prediction error relative to perfect-crystal models.
The proposed model explicitly includes defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
Separate machine-learning submodels will be trained for 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Electrical transport from 0–200 K is dominated by quantum and impurity scattering.
Electrical transport from 300–1200 K is dominated by phonon scattering and defect interactions.
HfNbTaTiZr can possess substantial intrinsic lattice distortion or defects associated with its multicomponent high-entropy-alloy structure.
Intrinsic lattice defects and oxygen impurities modify electron-scattering rates and electrical conductivity in a temperature-dependent manner.
At low temperature, defects and oxygen impurities enhance resistive scattering and may produce quantum-interference or localization effects.
At high temperature, phonon scattering combined with defects modifies electron mobility.
Machine-learning calibration against experimental conductivity data will refine the ab initio predictions.
The hybrid model will predict conductivity within approximately 20% of experiment in both specified temperature regimes.
Conventional analytical and ab initio perfect-crystal models deviate by more than 20% from measurements on defective HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model's claimed applicability is limited to bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Prediction accuracy will depend on the accuracy of the ab initio scattering calculations and the quality and range of the calibration data.
Conductivity deviations greater than 20% at either approximately 100 K or 800 K, or elsewhere in either regime, are proposed as a falsification criterion.
